questions.enonce_markdown:
Examine the circumstances that led to the compilation of the Glorious Qur'an.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Muslims believe that the Qur'an was revealed to the Prophet Muhammad over about twenty-three years, through the angel Jibril, from about 610 CE until shortly before his death in 632 CE. Its compilation into a single written volume took place in stages, in response to particular circumstances in the early caliphate.

**1. During the lifetime of the Prophet.**
- The revelations were memorised by the Prophet and many companions, who recited them in prayer. The Prophet had scribes (such as Zayd ibn Thabit, Ubayy ibn Ka'b and others) who wrote the verses on materials such as palm leaves, flat stones, leather, bones and pieces of cloth.
- The Prophet indicated the place of each revelation in its surah, and Jibril reviewed the whole with him, in particular in the last year of his life, according to tradition.
- The Qur'an was therefore complete, but it was not collected as one book, because revelation continued until near his death and because oral memorisation was the main method.

**2. Circumstances leading to the first compilation (the caliphate of Abu Bakr).**
- The death of the Prophet (632 CE) ended the revelation, so the text could now be gathered in final form.
- During the Ridda wars (wars against the apostate tribes and false prophets such as Musaylima) many of the companions who had memorised the Qur'an (huffaz) were killed, especially at the battle of Yamama.
- Umar ibn al-Khattab feared that large parts of the Qur'an might be lost with the death of more reciters, and urged Abu Bakr to have it collected. Abu Bakr was at first reluctant, as the Prophet had not done it, but he was persuaded that it was a good thing.
- Abu Bakr appointed Zayd ibn Thabit, a young scribe of the Prophet who had memorised the Qur'an, to collect it. Zayd searched for the written pieces and checked them against the memories of the companions, accepting a verse only when it was confirmed by witnesses. The pages (suhuf) were kept by Abu Bakr, then by Umar, and then by Hafsa, the daughter of Umar and wife of the Prophet.

**3. Circumstances leading to the standard copy (the caliphate of Uthman, 644-656 CE).**
- Islam spread rapidly into Syria, Iraq, Armenia, Egypt and beyond, and Muslims from different regions, with different dialects, recited the Qur'an in slightly different ways (the "seven ahruf", the modes of recitation permitted by the Prophet), and disputes arose among them.
- The companion Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, who had been with the army on the northern frontier, saw these disputes and warned Uthman to act before the community divided over its Book, as the Jews and Christians were said to have done.
- Uthman asked Hafsa to lend the pages. He appointed a committee including Zayd ibn Thabit and members of Quraysh to make copies, using the dialect of Quraysh where there was disagreement. The copies were sent to the main cities, along with a reciter, and other personal copies were ordered to be burned to prevent confusion.
- This is the text (the *mushaf* of Uthman) that Muslims have used since.

**4. Significance.** The compilation was a response to the need to preserve the Qur'an from loss and from disagreement. Muslims regard it as fulfilment of God's promise to preserve the Qur'an. Some Shi'a and Western scholars have raised questions about details of the accounts, but Muslims hold the Uthmanic text to be the one revealed.

**Conclusion.** The circumstances that led to the compilation were the death of the Prophet, the loss of reciters in the Ridda wars, and later the spread of Islam with differences of recitation. These led Abu Bakr and Uthman to collect and standardise the Book.
